passage.title: Reading Part 2 - Test 09
passage.text:
The human body is home to trillions of microorganisms—bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other microbes—collectively known as the microbiome. Far from being harmful invaders, most of these microscopic residents play vital roles in maintaining health. Recent scientific research has revealed that the microbiome influences everything from digestion and immune function to mental health and disease resistance, fundamentally changing our understanding of human biology.

The gut microbiome, which resides in the digestive system, has received particular attention from researchers. This complex ecosystem helps break down foods that the human body cannot digest on its own, particularly complex carbohydrates and fiber. In the process, these microbes produce vitamins, such as vitamin K and several B vitamins, that are essential for health. The gut microbiome also plays a crucial role in training and regulating the immune system. Studies have shown that people with diverse gut microbiomes tend to have stronger immune responses and lower rates of autoimmune diseases and allergies.

Perhaps most surprisingly, scientists have discovered a strong connection between the gut microbiome and the brain, often called the "gut-brain axis." The gut contains millions of neurons and produces many of the same neurotransmitters found in the brain, including serotonin, which regulates mood. Research suggests that the composition of the gut microbiome can influence mental health, with studies linking certain bacterial profiles to conditions such as depression, anxiety, and even autism. This connection may explain why many people experience digestive problems during times of stress or why certain probiotics—live beneficial bacteria—can improve mood.

However, modern lifestyles pose several threats to microbiome health. Overuse of antibiotics, while necessary to fight bacterial infections, can devastate the gut microbiome by killing beneficial bacteria along with harmful ones. Highly processed diets low in fiber fail to provide the nutrients that healthy gut bacteria need to thrive. Excessive hygiene practices, while important for preventing disease, may limit early-life exposure to microbes that help develop the immune system. Protecting and nurturing the microbiome requires a balanced approach: eating diverse, fiber-rich foods; using antibiotics only when necessary; and maintaining reasonable rather than excessive cleanliness. As research continues, our understanding of the microbiome's role in health will likely lead to new treatments for a wide range of conditions.
